PRESENTING A CLAIM TO A PUBLIC-ENTITY EMPLOYER BEFORE SUING OVER A TERMINATION (GOVERNMENT CLAIMS ACT, GOV. CODE §§ 905, 905.2, 910, 911.2, 911.4, 913, 915, 935, 945.4, 945.6, 950.2; STATE OF CALIFORNIA V. SUPERIOR COURT (BODDE); CITY OF STOCKTON V. SUPERIOR COURT; DICAMPLI-MINTZ V. COUNTY OF SANTA CLARA; WILLIAMS V. HORVATH) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee

WHAT THIS SHEET COVERS
This information sheet describes the claim-presentation machinery of the California Government Claims Act (Gov. Code, § 810 et seq.) as it bears on a suit for money against a public-entity employer arising out of the end of employment. Most material in this corpus on ending employment assumes a private employer that can simply be sued once a limitations period and any administrative exhaustion requirement are satisfied. When the employer is a public entity — a city, a county, a school or community college district, a special district, a state agency, the trial courts, or the California State University — a separate statutory step sits in front of the courthouse door: a written claim must be presented to the entity, and presented on time, before a suit for money or damages may be filed. The sheet sets out what the statutes say about which claims must be presented, to whom, in what form, by when, what happens when the deadline is missed, how long the claimant then has to sue, and how the requirement reaches individual public employees who are named as defendants. It also sets out what the California Supreme Court has held about the consequences of not presenting a claim. It states the law; it does not evaluate the position of Jordan Lee or of County of Example and does not say what either should do.

SECTION 945.4: PRESENTATION AND ACTION ON THE CLAIM AS A PRECONDITION TO SUIT
Government Code section 945.4 states the prohibition at the centre of the scheme. Except as provided in sections 946.4 and 946.6, the section provides that no suit for money or damages may be brought against a public entity on a cause of action for which a claim is required to be presented until a written claim has been presented to the entity and has been acted upon by the board, or has been deemed to have been rejected by the board. Two separate conditions therefore appear on the face of the section: presentation of a written claim, and either action on it or its rejection by operation of law. The section speaks of "money or damages"; it does not on its face reach an action seeking only non-monetary relief. Section 945.4 has not been amended since 1965.

SECTIONS 905 AND 905.2: WHICH CLAIMS MUST BE PRESENTED, AND THE EXCEPTION FOR EMPLOYEE WAGE CLAIMS
Two sections say which claims must be presented. For a local public entity — a city, a county, a school or community college district, a special district — Government Code section 905 provides that all claims for money or damages against local public entities shall be presented in accordance with the claim chapters, except for a list of categories set out in the section's subdivisions. For the State, Government Code section 905.2 applies instead: subdivision (a) provides that the section applies to claims against the state filed with the Department of General Services, apart from the stale-warrant claims described in subdivision (b)(2)(B), and subdivision (b) provides that all claims for money or damages against the state within the listed categories shall be presented in accordance with the claim chapters, paragraph (3) reaching claims for money or damages on express contract, or for an injury for which the state is liable. The state's channel is thus a centralised one, running to the Department of General Services rather than to the employing department. Four of the section 905 exceptions matter to a separation from public employment. Subdivision (c) excepts claims by public employees for fees, salaries, wages, mileage, or other expenses and allowances. Subdivision (d) excepts claims for which workers' compensation under Division 4 of the Labor Code is the exclusive remedy. Subdivision (f) excepts applications or claims for money or benefits under any public retirement or pension system. Subdivision (j) excepts claims arising under the Unemployment Insurance Code. The subdivision (c) exception is drawn by subject matter, not by who the defendant is: it turns on the character of what is claimed — fees, salaries, wages, mileage, or other expenses and allowances — rather than on the label attached to the cause of action.

SECTION 910: WHAT THE WRITTEN CLAIM MUST SHOW
Government Code section 910 provides that a claim shall be presented by the claimant or by a person acting on the claimant's behalf and shall show all of the items the section then lists: the claimant's name and post office address; the address to which notices are to be sent; the date, place and other circumstances of the occurrence or transaction giving rise to the claim; a general description of the indebtedness, obligation, injury, damage or loss incurred so far as it may be known at the time of presentation; the name or names of the public employee or employees causing the injury, damage or loss, if known; and the amount claimed, with its basis of computation, if that amount totals less than ten thousand dollars. Where the amount claimed exceeds ten thousand dollars, the section provides that no dollar amount shall be included in the claim, but that the claim shall indicate whether it would be a limited civil case.

SECTION 911.2: THE SIX-MONTH AND ONE-YEAR PRESENTATION DEADLINES
Government Code section 911.2, subdivision (a), divides claims into two classes. A claim relating to a cause of action for death or for injury to person or to personal property or growing crops shall be presented not later than six months after the accrual of the cause of action. A claim relating to any other cause of action shall be presented not later than one year after accrual. The line the section draws is therefore between personal-injury-type claims and everything else, not between tort and contract. Both deadlines run from accrual of the cause of action, and section 901 supplies the accrual rule by reference to the statute of limitations that would apply if no claim were required.

SECTION 915: WHERE THE CLAIM MUST BE DELIVERED — AND AN INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY IN SUBDIVISION (F)
Government Code section 915, subdivision (a), provides that a claim, any amendment to it, or an application for leave to present a late claim shall be presented to a local public entity by any of the following means: delivering it to the clerk, secretary, or auditor of the entity; mailing it to the clerk, secretary, auditor, or to the governing body at its principal office; or, if expressly authorized by an ordinance or resolution of the entity, submitting it electronically in the manner the ordinance or resolution specifies. Subdivision (b) routes claims against the state to the Department of General Services, subdivision (c) routes claims against judicial branch entities, and subdivision (d) routes claims against the Trustees of the California State University to the Office of Risk Management at the Chancellor's Office. Subdivision (f) contains a safe harbour keyed to the register of public agencies that the Secretary of State and county clerks maintain under Government Code section 53051. As currently codified, that subdivision is internally inconsistent: its operative sentence refers to the statement in the "Roster of Public Agencies," while the definitional sentence that follows defines the phrase "statement in the Registry of Public Agencies" — a phrase that appears nowhere else in the section.

SECTIONS 911.4 AND 946.6: APPLYING TO PRESENT A LATE CLAIM, AND PETITIONING THE COURT
Government Code section 911.4 supplies the route for a claim in the six-month class that was not presented in time. Subdivision (a) provides that when such a claim is not presented within that time, a written application may be made to the public entity for leave to present the claim. Subdivision (b) provides that the application shall be presented to the entity within a reasonable time not to exceed one year after accrual of the cause of action, shall state the reason for the delay, and shall have the proposed claim attached. Government Code section 946.6 supplies the judicial route that follows. Subdivision (a) provides that if an application for leave to present a claim is denied or deemed denied under section 911.6, a petition may be made to the court for an order relieving the petitioner from section 945.4. Subdivision (b) requires the petition to show that application was made to the board and was denied or deemed denied, the reason for the failure to present the claim within the section 911.2 period, and the information required by section 910, and provides that the petition shall be filed within six months after the application to the board is denied or deemed denied.

SECTIONS 913 AND 945.6: THE REJECTION NOTICE, ITS WARNING, AND THE DEADLINE TO SUE
Government Code section 913, subdivision (b), provides that if a claim is rejected in whole or in part, the notice of action must include a warning in substantially the form the section sets out: that, subject to certain exceptions, the claimant has only six months from the date the notice was personally delivered or deposited in the mail to file a court action on the claim, with a cross-reference to section 945.6, followed by a statement that the claimant may seek the advice of an attorney and, if so, should do so immediately. Government Code section 945.6, subdivision (a), then fixes the period. If written notice is given in accordance with section 913, suit must be commenced not later than six months after the date the notice is personally delivered or deposited in the mail. If written notice is not given in accordance with section 913, suit must be commenced within two years from the accrual of the cause of action. The period to sue is therefore keyed to the entity's own notice, and the entity's failure to give a conforming notice lengthens rather than shortens the claimant's window.

SECTION 950.2: THE BAR EXTENDS TO THE INDIVIDUAL PUBLIC EMPLOYEE
Government Code section 950.2 provides that, except as provided in section 950.4, a cause of action against a public employee or former public employee for injury resulting from an act or omission in the scope of that person's employment as a public employee is barred if an action against the employing public entity for that injury is barred under Part 3 (commencing with section 900) or under Chapter 2 (commencing with section 945) of Part 4. The section adds that it applies even though the public entity is itself immune from liability for the injury. The practical reach of the section is that naming a supervisor, manager or official personally does not by itself put the claim outside the presentation requirement where the conduct alleged was within the scope of public employment.

Code, § 810 et seq.) as it bears on a suit for money against a public-entity employer arising out of the end of employment. Most material in this corpus on ending employment assumes a private employer that can simply be sued once a limitations period and any administrative exhaustion requirement are satisfied. When the employer is a public entity — a city, a county, a school or community college district, a special district, a state agency, the trial courts, or the California State University — a separate statutory step sits in front of the courthouse door: a written claim must be presented to the entity, and presented on time, before a suit for money or damages may be filed. It states the law; it does not evaluate the position of Jordan Lee or of County of Example and does not say what either should do.

Government Code section 945.4 states the prohibition at the centre of the scheme. Except as provided in sections 946.4 and 946.6, the section provides that no suit for money or damages may be brought against a public entity on a cause of action for which a claim is required to be presented until a written claim has been presented to the entity and has been acted upon by the board, or has been deemed to have been rejected by the board. expectedJSON.body: In Williams v. Horvath (1976) 16 Cal.3d 834 the California Supreme Court considered whether a complaint filed in state court under 42 United States Code section 1983 must allege compliance with the claim requirement of the Government Code. Characterising the requirement as substantive rather than merely procedural — quoting Illerbrun v. Conrad for the proposition that the filing of a claim for damages is more than a procedural requirement, is a condition precedent to the plaintiff's maintaining an action against defendants, in short an integral part of the plaintiff's cause of action — the court held that the claim provision of section 911.2 is inoperative in an action brought under section 1983. The result is that a federal civil rights cause of action brought in a California court is not defeated by the absence of a presented claim, while a state-law cause of action joined in the same complaint remains subject to the requirement. The decision was unanimous; no separate opinion was filed.

citations.quote: Accordingly, we hold that the claim provision of section 911.2 is inoperative in an action brought under section 1983.

citations.case: Williams v. Horvath (quoting Illerbrun v. Conrad (1963) 216 Cal.App.2d 521, 524)

expectedJSON.gap: Williams was a police-misconduct case, not an employment case, and the opinion does not address employment separation. The opinion construes the 100-day claim period then in force; section 911.2 has since been amended and now sets six-month and one-year periods, so the holding survives the amendment but the opinion's description of the deadline does not match the current statute. That amendment postdates the opinion and is disclosed here rather than assumed away. The opinion's second holding — concerning a public entity's obligation to defend and indemnify its employees in a section 1983 action — is recorded as present but is not described or quoted here. Williams predates both Bodde and City of Stockton and uses the older "Tort Claims Act" label. The quoted Illerbrun passage reads "against defendants" in Williams; Bodde, quoting Williams, renders it in the singular. That discrepancy is described in the Bodde clause of this sheet, and the passage is quoted here from Williams, the earlier of the two opinions and the one closer to the source it quotes. Exact-phrase index queries on the Williams cluster returned 1 for "against defendants" and 0 for "against defendant"; two longer queries errored rather than returning a count and were re-run shorter, as recorded. The citation 16 Cal.3d 834 resolves to a single record, so unlike Bodde and City of Stockton there was no second cluster to compare. A second genuinely independent free publisher for this opinion could not be reached from this environment — Justia, FindLaw, Google Scholar, case.law, casetext, leagle and anylaw are all egress-blocked here — so "fetched twice" here means two different underlying texts served by one publisher, CourtListener, not two publishers.
